speaker_role: current admissions officer (University of Oregon) and current admissions officer (Beloit College), speaking at a high school info session
commercial_incentive: None evident; both speakers represent their own institutions, not a paid service
key_insights: Pushes back on the myth that admissions counselors are gatekeepers trying to keep students out; on average colleges nationally admit a large share of applicants
Notes the real stress point is not getting rejected everywhere but having to choose among multiple acceptances and 'break hearts' of other schools

Says the essay is the only part of the application that is the student's own voice, unlike grades/recommendations/activities, and that a well-written essay should make the reader want to meet the student
States a college recalculates transcripts and weighs performance closer to senior year more heavily than freshman year (freshman grades are least important)
Warns against padding activity lists with superficial involvement in many clubs; admissions prefers depth over breadth

Explains 'test optional' varies by school in practice; recommends students ask whether submitter vs non-submitter admit rates differ, whether opting out requires extra essays/interviews, and whether it affects scholarship eligibility
States University of Oregon is test-blind for scholarship consideration even if scores are on file for admission
Recommends applying after first-semester senior grades post for students with weaker prior GPA, versus applying early for consistently strong students
Advises students not to feel they must write an essay about trauma or hardship to be competitive, and that essays about someone else's story should still focus on why it matters to the student
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker (Sarah, U Oregon) states roughly 66% of all colleges/universities nationally admit about 66% of applicants on average
Speaker notes there are over 3,000 colleges/universities in the US
Speaker cites Northern Illinois University as fully test-blind (does not look at scores even if submitted)
Speaker states University of Oregon is test-blind specifically for scholarship decisions
notable_or_distinctive: Two admissions officers directly debunk the myth that going test-optional automatically helps or hurts, and give a specific checklist of questions (submitter vs non-submitter admit rates, extra requirements, scholarship impact) students should ask any test-optional school.
reliability_notes: Recorded during the pandemic-era shift to test-optional policies (2020-2021), so testing-policy specifics are dated; national admit-rate figure is presented without citation and audio has minor Zoom-era crosstalk.
